summary: Describes Topology Dissemination Based on Reverse-Path Forwarding (TBRPF), a proactive link-state routing protocol for mobile ad hoc networks that provides hop-by-hop shortest-path routing. Each node computes a source tree from partial topology information, and the protocol is designed to keep overhead low. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: TBRPF helps moving wireless routers find routes to reachable destinations. Each router shares only part of its route information and sends smaller updates when that information changes.

questions: link state routing for ad hoc networks
how does tbrpf differ from ospf
how does tbrpf reduce routing traffic
subtitle: A proactive routing protocol that limits control traffic in mobile ad hoc networks.

tldr.problem: Mobile ad hoc networks change as wireless links appear and disappear. Repeatedly sending a full network map can use too much of the shared radio capacity.
tldr.mechanism: Each node computes shortest paths from partial topology information, reports only a subtree to neighbors, and sends periodic full updates plus smaller change updates. HELLO messages also report neighbor-state changes.
tldr.outcome: TBRPF is an Experimental routing protocol for MANETs. RFC 3684 has been updated by RFC 9141.

today: RFC 3684 is an Experimental specification and is updated by RFC 9141. It has not been obsoleted according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: Routes from Partial Topology Information
sections.content:
Topology Dissemination Based on Reverse-Path Forwarding (TBRPF) is a proactive link-state routing protocol for mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs). Each node keeps routes to reachable destinations and computes a source tree using a modified form of Dijkstra's algorithm.

To reduce overhead, a node reports only part of its source tree, called its reported subtree. Neighbors use those reports to update their own topology information. The protocol can also report extra links when additional robustness is wanted.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router calculates paths using the network information it has received. It shares only the part of its route tree that neighbors need for their own calculations.

sections.title: Packets and Neighbor Messages
sections.content:
A TBRPF packet has a header and a body containing one or more messages. The header can include the packet length and router ID when the underlying delivery service does not provide them. Message types identify HELLO information, topology updates, or address associations.

Neighbor discovery uses three HELLO message types: NEIGHBOR REQUEST, NEIGHBOR REPLY, and NEIGHBOR LOST. Each reports relevant neighbor interface addresses and carries a HELLO sequence number. Receivers process packet elements in order and discard unprocessed elements after detecting a malformed one.
sections.plainLanguage: Every packet identifies the type of information it carries. HELLO messages tell neighbors when a link is being requested, confirmed, or reported lost.

sections.title: How Nodes Confirm Neighbor Links
sections.content:
TBRPF neighbor discovery records a link as LOST, 1-WAY, or 2-WAY. A node waits for enough recent HELLO messages before treating a link as one-way. It then requests confirmation, and the neighbor's reply lets both sides mark the link as bidirectional.

A node announces a lost link when it misses the configured number of HELLO messages or the neighbor-hold timer expires. By default, HELLO messages are sent at least once per second, and the default neighbor-hold time is three seconds. A link-layer failure report can also trigger a loss announcement.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers exchange HELLO messages to check whether each can hear the other. Missing enough messages or reaching the timeout changes the link to lost.

sections.title: Periodic and Differential Route Updates
sections.content:
Each node calculates routes from its topology graph and sends periodic and differential updates. A periodic update reports the full reported subtree; a differential update reports additions and deletions. The default intervals are five seconds for periodic updates and one second for differential updates.

TBRPF does not require acknowledgments or sequenced delivery for topology updates. Instead, it uses reports from the next hop toward a link's tail and expires old topology information. A node may also advertise interface addresses, host addresses, and network prefixes associated with a router ID.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers send a complete report at intervals and smaller reports when routes change. Old information expires so a router can stop using links that are no longer reported.

sections.title: Security on Wireless Links
sections.content:
The RFC notes that wireless networks make it harder to control who can join and easier to observe or interfere with traffic. It points to link-layer security for controlling connections and says routing-domain members need authentication and authorization through a separate system.

OSPF-OR can use the IPv6 Authentication Header and Encapsulating Security Payload for authentication, integrity, and confidentiality. Those mechanisms do not protect against a compromised, malfunctioning, or misconfigured router.
sections.plainLanguage: Nearby devices may be able to hear or disrupt wireless routing messages. The RFC points to authentication and encryption mechanisms, while noting that compromised routers remain a risk.
